rv.q: So it is with this new play by Gurpreet Kaur Bhatti – even if the narrative is tinged with dramatic contrivance.

It is a thought-provoking production and a strong example of Clean Break’s commitment to using theatre to challenge stereotypes and encourage audiences to reflect on women’s experiences of inequality.
Baby is a challenging but hugely informative and emotional piece of work that resounds with authenticity.
Vulnerable, funny and quietly devastating, Pearl Mackie gives a powerhouse performance in this deeply human one-woman drama .
Mackie is extremely engaging, often funny, sometimes tragic, always passionate in her emotionally detailed delivery.
Like its titular heroine, Baby is beautiful and brilliant, if a bit rough around the edges.
Standing tall above the bureaucracy, the files and an uncaring system, she proves herself to her audience, in a sobering piece of theatre.
Baby is often very funny and deeply touching, carried by a performance that makes its small stage feel alive with possibility.
Pearl Mackie is ‘Baby’ and what an incredible job she does.

Mackie formidably commands Khadija Raza’s clinical, butter-yellow set, filling its stripped-back space with the haunting weight of her memories; though her performance sometimes verges on staccato in moments when she must also serve as her own stagehand.
Uneven in places, but anchored by a remarkable central performance, Baby is an urgent, compassionate piece of theatre that lingers beyond the final curtain.

cn.t: Pearl Mackie delivers a magnetic, commanding performance in this powerful but occasionally contrived one-woman show about motherhood and the prison system, with critics praising her charisma while noting the narrative's dramatic contrivances.
